notes.b: A volcano is an opening (vent) in the Earth's crust, the thin rocky outer layer, through which magma, gases and fragments escape, together with the landform built around it. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is magma that has reached the surface.
points: Magma chamber: the reservoir of magma beneath the volcano, where the molten rock collects before it rises.
Main vent: the pipe (conduit) that carries magma up to the crater.
Secondary (parasitic) vent: a smaller opening on the flanks (sides) of the cone, which lets magma escape away from the summit.
Crater: the hollow at the top of the main vent.
Cone: the hill of the volcano, built up over many eruptions from alternating layers of lava and ash.
Lava flow: lava moving across the surface away from the vent, such as the flows drawn down the side of the cone.

Diagram: draw a labelled cross-section showing the magma chamber, main vent, secondary vent, crater, cone of alternating lava and ash layers, lava flow, ash cloud and volcanic bombs, with the crust around the chamber.
notes.tip: Keep magma and lava apart: magma is below ground, lava is on the surface. For a labelling question, you need to name every part of the cross-section: magma chamber, main vent, secondary vent, crater, layers of lava and ash, ash cloud, volcanic bomb, crust and flowing lava.

notes.h: Materials ejected and the hazards they cause
notes.b: An eruption throws out liquid, gas and solid material. Each one is a hazard in its own right, so you need to know the names and what each does.
points: Lava: molten rock that flows from the vent, so it can bury land and buildings around the volcano.
Gases: water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide, which are released as the magma rises and the pressure on it falls.
Pyroclastic material (tephra): solid fragments of rock thrown into the air. It includes ash, lapilli (cinders), volcanic bombs and pumice.
Ash: the finest pyroclastic particles, which are light enough to fall over wide areas.
Volcanic bombs: large lumps of lava thrown out of the vent while still partly molten.
Pumice: a light, porous rock (full of tiny holes) formed from frothy lava.
Pyroclastic flows: fast, very hot avalanches of gas, ash and rock moving down the slopes, so they destroy anything in their path.
Lahars: volcanic mudflows of ash and water, for example when an eruption melts snow or ice.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to name two materials released in an eruption, two gases, or two pyroclastic materials. Choose from the lists above: for example, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide as gases, ash and pumice as pyroclastic material.

notes.b: The silica content of magma (silica is the mineral material that makes rock) controls how runny the lava is, how much gas it traps, and so how the volcano erupts.
points: Basic (basaltic) lava is low in silica and hot, so it is runny (low viscosity, meaning it flows easily).
Gases escape easily from basic lava, so eruptions are gentle (effusive, meaning lava pours out rather than blasting).
Acidic lava is high in silica and cooler, so it is viscous (thick and sticky).
Acidic lava traps gas, so pressure builds up and eruptions are explosive.

Low-viscosity lava spreads widely and builds shield volcanoes (broad, gently sloping); viscous lava piles up into steep cones. The names and shapes of the landform types belong to the volcanic and plutonic landforms notes.
notes.tip: Pair each lava type with its eruption style and give the reason: basic means runny, gases escape and the eruption is gentle; acidic means viscous, gas is trapped and the eruption is explosive.

notes.b: Volcanoes are grouped by how likely they are to erupt again. The groups depend on how long it has been since the last eruption and whether another is expected.
points: Active: a volcano that has erupted recently and may erupt again soon. Examples: Mount Etna, Sicily, Italy; Kilauea, Hawaii; Stromboli, Italy.
Dormant (sleeping): a volcano that has not erupted for a long time but could erupt again. Example: Mount Fuji, Japan, last erupted in 1707.
Extinct: a volcano not expected ever to erupt again. Example: Slemish, Co. Antrim, the remains of an extinct volcano, linked with St Patrick.
notes.tip: Dormant is not the same as extinct: a dormant volcano can erupt again, an extinct one is not expected to. Mount Fuji is dormant, not extinct. Questions ask you to define all three and to choose dormant or extinct for a given volcano.

notes.b: Most volcanoes lie in narrow belts that follow plate boundaries (the lines where the huge slabs of crust, called plates, meet), not at random. Each type of boundary gives a different result.
points: Constructive (divergent) boundaries: basic magma rises to fill the gap where plates separate, mostly under the sea along mid-ocean ridges (underwater mountain chains).
Iceland is where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level; the North American and Eurasian plates are moving apart there.
Destructive (convergent) boundaries: oceanic crust is subducted (pushed down beneath another plate), the descending plate melts, and acidic magma rises to form explosive volcanoes.
Destructive boundaries form volcanoes in fold-mountain chains (mountains crumpled up where plates collide), such as the Andes where the Nazca plate is subducted beneath the South American plate.
They also form volcanoes in island arcs (curved chains of volcanic islands) such as Japan and Indonesia.
Continental-continental collision and transform (conservative) boundaries, where plates slide past each other, have few or no volcanoes, so magma rarely reaches the surface there.
notes.tip: The 30-mark question asks how plate tectonics explains where volcanoes are found. Go boundary by boundary: say where volcanoes occur and why, and name an example such as Iceland or the Andes. Iceland sits on the North American and Eurasian plates.

notes.b: A belt of volcanoes circles the Pacific Ocean, because most of the plate boundaries around that ocean are destructive.
points: The Ring of Fire is a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, mainly along destructive boundaries.
It contains about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes.
Examples: Mount St Helens (Cascade Range, Washington State, USA); Mount Fuji, Japan; Mount Pinatubo, the Philippines; Krakatoa, Indonesia; volcanoes of the Andes.
notes.tip: The Ring of Fire is around the Pacific, not the Atlantic. Questions ask what it is and what occurs there: volcanoes and many earthquakes. Use the figure about three-quarters of active volcanoes and no other percentage.

notes.b: A hot spot is a plume of magma rising from deep in the mantle (the hot layer beneath the crust), away from plate boundaries. It explains volcanoes in places where no plates meet.
points: As a plate moves over a stationary hot spot, a chain of volcanoes forms, with the volcanoes getting older with distance from the hot spot, because each one is carried away from the magma supply.
Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific plate over a hot spot, so it is not on a plate boundary. The Pacific plate moves north-west, so the islands get older to the north-west.
The active volcanoes Kilauea and Mauna Loa are on the Big Island in the south-east, over the hot spot.
Other hot spots: Yellowstone, USA; Iceland, which is on a constructive boundary and also over a hot spot.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name a volcanic hot spot: Hawaii is the example to use, because it is a hot spot and not on a plate boundary. Iceland is on a constructive boundary and over a hot spot.

notes.b: Ireland has no active volcanoes now, but it had huge eruptions in the past. These were linked to the opening of the North Atlantic Ocean, which is the syllabus's national setting.
points: Ireland lies in the middle of the Eurasian plate, far from a plate boundary, so it has no active volcanoes today.
About 60 million years ago, North America and Greenland separated from Europe as the Atlantic opened. The crust stretched and cracked.
Basic lava poured out of long fissures (cracks in the ground) in north-east Ireland, flow upon flow, in fissure eruptions. These lavas formed the Antrim basalts.
Basalt is an extrusive (volcanic) rock, meaning it formed from lava on the surface. The Antrim basalts came from fissures, not from a single cone volcano.
Landforms from these lavas include the Antrim plateau and the Giant's Causeway.
notes.tip: To link Antrim to the Atlantic, give the cause: the plates separated, the crust stretched and cracked, and basic lava poured out of fissures. Basalt is volcanic (extrusive), not plutonic, and it came from fissures, not one cone.

notes.b: Eruptions can kill people and damage land, buildings, travel and even the climate. Named examples show how large the damage can be.
points: Loss of life, and destruction of buildings, farmland and infrastructure by lava, pyroclastic flows and lahars. In AD 79 Vesuvius, near Naples, Italy, buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flows.
In 2018, lava from Kilauea's lower East Rift Zone destroyed hundreds of homes in the Leilani Estates area of Hawaii.
Ash fall can collapse roofs under its weight, for example when thick ash builds up on them, destroy crops and contaminate water supplies.
Ash clouds disrupt air travel. In April 2010 an eruption under the Eyjafjallajökull ice cap, Iceland, closed much of European airspace for about a week, and about 100,000 flights were cancelled.
Volcanic tsunamis (huge sea waves): the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, Indonesia, caused tsunamis that killed about 36,000 people.
The undersea Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcano, Tonga, erupted on 15 January 2022 and caused a tsunami across the Pacific.

Gases and ash can cool the global climate for a year or two. After Mount Pinatubo, the Philippines, erupted in 1991, sulphur dioxide in the upper atmosphere cooled global average temperatures by about 0.5°C over the following year or so.
Economic losses and evacuation of populations, because homes, farms and businesses are lost and people must leave the danger zone.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions on negative effects carry 13 to 14 marks, with shorter answers at Higher Level. Give each effect with a named example such as Vesuvius, Krakatoa or Eyjafjallajökull.

notes.b: Volcanoes are dangerous, but they also give people land, energy, income and materials. This is why many people live close to them.
points: Fertile soils from weathered volcanic ash and lava, which break down into minerals plants can use. On the slopes of Mount Etna and Vesuvius they support vineyards and orchards.
Geothermal energy (heat from underground) and hot water: in Iceland geothermal energy heats about nine in ten homes and generates electricity.
Tourism: volcanoes, geysers (jets of hot water and steam) and hot springs attract visitors, such as the Blue Lagoon and the geysers at Geysir, Iceland.
Minerals and building materials, such as sulphur, pumice and basalt, which can be quarried or mined from volcanic rock.
New land: Surtsey, an island that emerged from the sea off southern Iceland in 1963.
notes.tip: Positive effects are asked alongside negative effects, at 13 to 14 marks each at Ordinary Level. Name an example with each one, such as Iceland for geothermal energy and Surtsey for new land.

notes.h: Case study: Mount St Helens, 1980 (setting and sequence)
notes.b: Mount St Helens is the full case study to learn, with date, place, plate setting, events, effects and response. The eruption was sideways, not vertical, which makes it unusual.
points: Place: Cascade Range, Washington State, USA. The Juan de Fuca plate is subducted beneath the North American plate, a destructive boundary.
For weeks before 18 May 1980, magma pushed the north flank (side) outwards into a bulge.
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the collapse of the north flank as a huge landslide.
The collapse released a sideways (lateral) blast that flattened forests.
The summit lost about 400 m of height, leaving a horseshoe-shaped crater.
notes.tip: The 1980 eruption was a lateral (sideways) blast after a landslide, not a vertical one. Give the date, place, plate setting, the sequence of events, the effects and the response.

notes.h: Case study: Mount St Helens, 1980 (effects and response)
notes.b: The eruption did great damage, but the number of deaths was low because people had been kept away from the danger zone.
points: Ash fell across several US states.
Lahars (mudflows of ash and water) flowed down river valleys, including the Toutle River, destroying bridges and homes.
57 people died, not thousands.
Most people had been kept out of a restricted zone, which kept the death toll low.
notes.tip: Give the response with the effects: the restricted zone is why the death toll was 57 and not far higher.

notes.b: Volcanoes usually give warning signs, because magma must move upwards before an eruption. Scientists measure these signs to judge when a volcano is becoming dangerous.
points: Seismometers (instruments that record earthquakes) pick up swarms of small earthquakes as magma rises.
Ground deformation: tiltmeters (which measure changes in slope), GPS and satellite radar measure swelling or bulging of the cone.
Gas emissions: changes in the amount and type of gas, especially sulphur dioxide.
Temperature: thermal imaging and satellites detect heating of the ground or of crater lakes.
Changes in groundwater and springs, for example because rising magma heats the water underground.
Studying the deposits and records of past eruptions shows how often a volcano erupts and which areas are at risk. Hazard maps show these areas.
Scientists can often forecast that an eruption is likely, but not its exact time, size or style.
notes.tip: Questions ask for two ways eruptions can be predicted. Pick two methods from the list and say what each measures, such as seismometers recording small earthquakes or tiltmeters measuring swelling.

notes.b: Eruptions cannot be stopped, but their effects can be limited. The main approaches are to watch the volcano, keep people out of danger, and sometimes to fight the lava itself.
points: Monitoring by volcano observatories, so that warning signs are picked up early.
Hazard zoning keeps settlement out of high-risk zones, so fewer people and buildings are in the path of an eruption.
Evacuation plans and warning systems, and public education.
Diverting or slowing lava flows with barriers and channels, or cooling it with water.

Heimaey, Iceland, 1973: the Eldfell eruption on Heimaey, Westman Islands, threatened the harbour. About 5,000 residents were evacuated overnight, mostly by the fishing fleet. Sea water was pumped onto the advancing lava to cool and halt it, saving the harbour.

Pinatubo, the Philippines, 1991: scientists from the US Geological Survey and the Philippine volcano institute monitored earthquakes, gas emissions and swelling, and forecast the eruption. Tens of thousands of people were evacuated, including from the US Clark Air Base, saving thousands of lives.
notes.tip: Questions ask for one way to limit damage from an eruption. Name the measure and back it with an example: Heimaey for cooling lava with sea water, Pinatubo for a successful forecast and evacuation.

keyTerms.definition: Molten rock below the earth's surface.
Magma that has reached the surface through a vent.
An opening in the crust through which magma, gases and fragments escape.
Solid fragments thrown into the air by an eruption, including ash, lapilli, volcanic bombs and pumice.
A fast, very hot avalanche of gas, ash and rock moving down a volcano's slopes.
A volcanic mudflow of ash and water.
Low-silica, hot, runny lava from which gases escape easily, producing gentle eruptions.
High-silica, cooler, viscous lava that traps gas, producing explosive eruptions.
A volcano that has erupted recently and may erupt again soon.
A volcano that has not erupted for a long time but could erupt again.
A volcano not expected ever to erupt again.
A belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the edges of the Pacific Ocean.
A plume of magma rising from deep in the mantle, away from plate boundaries, which can form a chain of volcanoes as a plate moves over it.
An eruption of lava from a long crack in the crust, as in the Antrim basalts.

factCards.term: Volcano diagram: the parts to label
factCards.definition: Magma chamber; main vent (pipe or conduit); secondary (parasitic) vent on the flank; crater at the top of the main vent; cone of alternating layers of lava and ash; lava flow; ash cloud; volcanic bombs.

factCards.term: Name three gases released in a volcanic eruption
factCards.definition: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide. They escape easily from runny basic lava, but viscous acidic lava traps them, which makes eruptions explosive.

factCards.term: Active, dormant and extinct volcanoes: an example of each
factCards.definition: Active: Mount Etna, Sicily; Kilauea, Hawaii; Stromboli, Italy. Dormant: Mount Fuji, Japan, which last erupted in 1707. Extinct: Slemish, Co. Antrim, the hill linked with St Patrick.

factCards.term: Why volcanoes form at constructive and destructive boundaries
factCards.definition: Constructive: basic magma rises where plates separate, mostly along mid-ocean ridges under the sea. Destructive: subducted oceanic crust melts and acidic magma rises to form explosive volcanoes in fold mountains (the Andes) or island arcs (Japan, Indonesia).

factCards.term: Volcanoes: which boundaries have few, and why Ireland has none today
factCards.definition: Continental–continental collision boundaries and transform (conservative) boundaries have few or no volcanoes. Ireland lies in the middle of the Eurasian plate, far from any boundary, so it has no active volcanoes.

factCards.term: Iceland: plate setting and two named volcanoes
factCards.definition: Iceland is where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level, with the North American and Eurasian plates moving apart; it also lies over a hot spot. Its volcanoes include Hekla and Eyjafjallajökull.

factCards.term: Ring of Fire volcanoes: share and four named examples
factCards.definition: A belt, mainly of destructive boundaries, around the edges of the Pacific with about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes, including Mount St Helens, USA; Mount Fuji, Japan; Mount Pinatubo, the Philippines; and Krakatoa, Indonesia.

factCards.term: Hawaii hot spot: how the island chain forms
factCards.definition: Hawaii sits mid-Pacific plate over a stationary hot spot. The plate moves north-west, so the islands get older to the north-west; the active volcanoes, Kilauea and Mauna Loa, are on the Big Island in the south-east. Other hot spots: Yellowstone, Iceland.

factCards.term: Antrim basalts: cause, type of eruption and date
factCards.definition: As North America and Greenland separated from Europe with the opening of the Atlantic, the crust stretched and cracked; basic lava poured out of long fissures in north-east Ireland, flow upon flow, about 60 million years ago.

factCards.term: Mount St Helens, 1980: setting and sequence of events
factCards.definition: Cascade Range, Washington State, USA, where the Juan de Fuca plate subducts beneath the North American plate. For weeks magma bulged the north flank; on 18 May a magnitude 5.1 earthquake collapsed it in a huge landslide, releasing a sideways blast.

factCards.term: Mount St Helens, 1980: effects and why few died
factCards.definition: The sideways blast flattened forests; the summit lost about 400 m, leaving a horseshoe-shaped crater; ash fell across several US states; lahars down the Toutle River destroyed bridges and homes. 57 died; most people had been kept out of a restricted zone.

factCards.term: Negative effects of volcanoes: three named examples
factCards.definition: Vesuvius, AD 79, buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flows. Krakatoa, 1883: tsunamis killed about 36,000 people. Eyjafjallajökull, April 2010: an ash cloud closed much of European airspace for about a week; about 100,000 flights cancelled.

factCards.term: Mount Pinatubo, 1991: effect on global climate
factCards.definition: Sulphur dioxide from the eruption in the Philippines reached the upper atmosphere and cooled global average temperatures by about 0.5°C over the following year or so.

factCards.term: Positive effects of volcanoes: five, with examples
factCards.definition: Fertile soils (vineyards and orchards on Etna and Vesuvius); geothermal energy, which heats about nine in ten homes in Iceland; tourism (the Blue Lagoon, Geysir); new land (Surtsey, 1963); minerals and building materials such as sulphur, pumice and basalt.

Seismometers record swarms of small earthquakes as magma rises; tiltmeters, GPS and satellite radar measure swelling of the cone; gas monitoring tracks changes, especially in sulphur dioxide; thermal imaging detects heating of the ground or crater lakes.

factCards.term: Eruption prediction: the use of past eruptions, and the limits
factCards.definition: Deposits and records of past eruptions show how often a volcano erupts and which areas are at risk, shown on hazard maps. Scientists can often forecast that an eruption is likely, but not its exact time, size or style.

factCards.term: Reducing the effects of eruptions: four methods
factCards.definition: Monitoring by volcano observatories; hazard zoning to keep settlement out of high-risk zones; evacuation plans, warning systems and public education; diverting or slowing lava with barriers and channels, or cooling it with water.

factCards.term: Heimaey, 1973: how the harbour was saved
factCards.definition: During the Eldfell eruption on Heimaey, Westman Islands, Iceland, about 5,000 residents were evacuated overnight, mostly by the fishing fleet, and sea water was pumped onto the advancing lava to cool and halt it.

Scientists from the US Geological Survey and the Philippine volcano institute monitored earthquakes, gas emissions and swelling and forecast the eruption; tens of thousands were evacuated, including from the US Clark Air Base, saving thousands of lives.

questions.prompt: Explain how plate tectonics helps us to understand the global distribution of volcanoes.
questions.model: Volcanoes lie in belts along plate boundaries. At constructive boundaries basic magma rises where plates separate, as at Iceland on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the ridge rises above sea level. At destructive boundaries oceanic crust is subducted and the melted plate produces acidic magma and explosive volcanoes: the Andes, where the Nazca plate is subducted beneath the South American plate, and island arcs such as Japan and Indonesia. The Pacific Ring of Fire follows these destructive boundaries and holds about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes. Continental collision and transform boundaries have few or no volcanoes. Hot spots such as Hawaii form volcanoes away from plate boundaries, with the islands getting older to the north-west as the Pacific plate moves over the hot spot. Ireland lies in the middle of the Eurasian plate, far from a boundary, so it has no active volcanoes, but its Antrim basalts were erupted about 60 million years ago as the Atlantic opened.

questions.prompt: Discuss the positive and negative effects of volcanoes, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Negative effects: loss of life and destruction of buildings and farmland by lava, pyroclastic flows and lahars, for example Vesuvius burying Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79; ash fall collapsing roofs and contaminating water; ash clouds disrupting air travel, for example the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption, which closed European airspace for about a week; volcanic tsunamis, for example Krakatoa in 1883, which killed about 36,000 people; and climate cooling after Mount Pinatubo in 1991, when sulphur dioxide cooled global average temperatures by about 0.5°C. Positive effects: fertile soils on the slopes of Mount Etna and Vesuvius that support vineyards and orchards; geothermal energy, which heats about nine in ten homes in Iceland; tourism, such as the Blue Lagoon and the geysers at Geysir; minerals and building materials such as sulphur, pumice and basalt; and new land, such as Surtsey, which emerged from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which volcanic eruptions can be predicted, and one way their effects can be reduced.
questions.model: Seismic monitoring: seismometers record swarms of small earthquakes, which show magma moving upwards before an eruption. Ground deformation: tiltmeters, GPS and satellite radar measure the swelling of the cone as magma pushes into it. Evidence that these methods work comes from Mount Pinatubo in 1991, where scientists monitored earthquakes, gas emissions and swelling, forecast the eruption, and evacuated tens of thousands of people. The effects can be reduced by cooling lava: at Heimaey, Iceland, in 1973, sea water was pumped onto the advancing lava to cool and halt it, saving the harbour.
